learning.javascript:
Going through a string

A for...of loop visits a string's characters one at a time, in order. Each c is a one-character string:

for (const c of s) {
    console.log(c);   // "H", then "i", then "!" when s is "Hi!"
}

Inside the loop you can do anything with c, such as adding it to a new string, as below.

Strings can't be changed: build a new one

JavaScript strings are immutable: once made, a string never changes. Assigning to s[0] doesn't change s (it's ignored, or in strict mode it throws a TypeError). Instead, build a new string from pieces:

let result = "";
result += "h";            // each += makes a new, longer string
result += "I";            // "hI"

const parts = [];         // or collect pieces in an array
parts.push("h");
parts.push("I");
parts.join("");           // "hI"

Either way is fine for strings of this size.
learning.python:
Going through a string

A for loop visits a string's characters one at a time, in order. Each c is a one-character string:

for c in s:
    print(c)          # "H", then "i", then "!" when s is "Hi!"

Inside the loop you can do anything with c, such as adding it to a new string, as below.

Strings can't be changed: build a new one

Python strings are immutable: once made, a string never changes. s[0] = "H" raises TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment. Instead, build a new string from pieces:

result = ""
result += "h"             # each += makes a new, longer string
result += "I"             # "hI"

parts = []                # or collect pieces in a list
parts.append("h")
parts.append("I")
"".join(parts)            # "hI"

Either way is fine for strings of this size. "".join(...) is the usual Python idiom. See str.join().
learning.cpp:
Going through a string

A range-based for loop visits a std::string's characters one at a time, in order. Each c is a char:

for (char c : s) {
    cout << c << endl;   // 'H', then 'i', then '!' when s is "Hi!"
}

Inside the loop you can do anything with c, such as adding it to a new string, as below.

A std::string can be changed

Unlike strings in JavaScript, Python, Java and D, a C++ std::string is mutable: s[0] = 'H'; changes it. Here s is passed by value, so the function has its own copy, and you can change it and return it. To change the characters in a loop, take each one by reference, with &:

for (char c : s)  { c = 'x'; }   // changes a copy of each char: s is unchanged
for (char& c : s) { c = 'x'; }   // changes s itself

You can also build a new string: string result; result += 'h'; or result.push_back('h');.
learning.java:
Going through a string

A for-each loop over s.toCharArray() visits a String's characters one at a time, in order. Each c is a char:

for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
    System.out.println(c);   // 'H', then 'i', then '!' when s is "Hi!"
}

Inside the loop you can do anything with c, such as adding it to a new string, as below.

Strings can't be changed: build a new one

Java Strings are immutable: once made, a String never changes, and there's no method that changes one. Build a new one instead, either with a StringBuilder or from a char array:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
sb.append('h');
sb.append('I');
sb.toString();                  // "hI"

char[] chars = s.toCharArray();  // a copy you can change
chars[0] = 'H';
new String(chars);              // a new String from the array

See String and StringBuilder in the Java 21 documentation.
learning.d:
Going through a string

A foreach loop visits a string's characters one at a time, in order. Each c is a char:

foreach (c; s) {
    writeln(c);   // 'H', then 'i', then '!' when s is "Hi!"
}

Inside the loop you can do anything with c, such as adding it to a new string, as below.

Strings can't be changed: build a new one

In D, string means immutable(char)[]: an array of characters that can't be changed, so s[0] = 'H'; doesn't compile. Either make a changeable copy and turn it back into a string at the end, or build a new one by appending:

char[] buf = s.dup;     // .dup: a changeable copy
buf[0] = 'H';
return buf.idup;        // .idup: an immutable copy, which is a string

string result;
result ~= 'h';          // ~= appends
result ~= 'I';          // "hI"

See Strings in the D language specification.

Given a string s, return a new string in which every character of s appears twice in a row, in the same order. Spaces, digits and punctuation are doubled too.
